candidate.answerReason: The roots have product 2010 and sum a. A prime factor of 67 forces one root to be at least 67; the optimal remaining factor pair is 5 and 6, giving a=78.

methods.label: Use the large prime factor
methods.explanation:
Let the positive integer roots be \(u,v,w\). Expanding their linear factors shows why the coefficients give useful information:
\[
(x-u)(x-v)(x-w)
=x^3-(u+v+w)x^2
+(uv+uw+vw)x-uvw.
\]
Comparing with the given polynomial yields
\[
a=u+v+w,\qquad uvw=2010.
\]
Thus we want the smallest sum of three positive integer factors whose product is \(2010\).

Factor the product:
\[
2010=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot67.
\]
The prime factor \(67\) must occur in at least one root. The roots \(5,6,67\) already give the candidate sum \(78\). If a root divisible by \(67\) were larger than \(67\), it would be at least \(134\), making the sum greater than \(78\). Therefore any equally good or better choice must have a root equal to \(67\).

The other two roots must then have product \(2010/67=30\). Up to reversing their order, all positive integer factor pairs are
\[
(1,30),\quad(2,15),\quad(3,10),\quad(5,6).
\]
Their sums are \(31,17,13,11\), respectively, so the smallest is \(11\), attained by \(5\) and \(6\). Consequently,
\[
a_{\min}=67+5+6=\boxed{78},
\]
choice \(\text{A}\). The product \((x-5)(x-6)(x-67)\) supplies a polynomial satisfying all the original root conditions.

Prime factorization supports the decisive large-root restriction, while the method's factor-pair search handles the remaining integer equation exhaustively. Polynomial expansion supplies the coefficient identities without requiring quadratic Vieta or AM-GM as separate prerequisites.

review.mathematicalCheck: Expansion gives a=u+v+w and uvw=2010. Since 67 is prime, some root is divisible by 67. Any such root exceeding 67 already exceeds the candidate sum 78. With root 67, the exhaustive factor pairs of 30 have minimum sum 11 at 5 and 6. These roots realize a=78.
